stem: You are the medicine registrar called to ED to review a 56-year-old man with type 2 diabetes who presents with a 36-hour history of escalating left lower limb pain. He noticed redness yesterday after a minor abrasion. The pain has rapidly worsened overnight, out of proportion to the visible erythema. He is now febrile and confused. Examination shows tense oedema, dusky skin discolouration with one violaceous patch, and crepitus on palpation. The team is debating cellulitis versus necrotising fasciitis.

data_table.Examination: Tense oedema entire calf; dusky discolouration with violaceous patch; crepitus on palpation; pain disproportionate to visible erythema; reduced sensation over dusky area
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22 (neutrophils 18), CRP 320, sodium 128, glucose 18, creatinine 156, lactate 5.2; venous gas: pH 7.28, lactate 5.2; LRINEC score 9
data_table.Medications: Metformin 1 g BD; gliclazide 60 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Urgent surgical consultation for emergency debridement; broad-spectrum IV antibiotics including clindamycin; aggressive resuscitation
options.rationale: Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency; immediate debridement, broad antibiotics with anti-toxin coverage (clindamycin) and aggressive resuscitation reduce mortality; LRINEC 8 or above and pain out of proportion are red flags. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Commence oral cefalexin 500 mg every 6 hours for cellulitis; mark the erythema and review in 24 hours
options.rationale: Oral cellulitis treatment is inappropriate for systemic toxicity, crepitus, dusky skin and disproportionate pain; necrotising fasciitis demands surgical and IV antibiotic emergency response. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Administer IV vancomycin alone; defer surgical consultation pending blood culture results to confirm a microbiological diagnosis
options.rationale: Antibiotic alone without surgical debridement does not control necrotising soft tissue infection; surgical exploration is the diagnostic and therapeutic gold standard. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Order urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the limb and defer empirical antibiotics until imaging confirms fascial involvement
options.rationale: Imaging delays definitive surgical management; clinical suspicion plus LRINEC 8+ mandates immediate surgical consultation regardless of imaging. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Elevate the limb, commence subcutaneous low molecular weight heparin and observe over 6 hours for spread of erythema
options.rationale: Observation in suspected necrotising fasciitis is fatal; hourly progression of fascial necrosis demands immediate surgical exploration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency with mortality of 20 to 40 percent. Clinical clues: pain out of proportion to skin findings, rapid progression, dusky or violaceous skin, crepitus, bullae, anaesthesia over the involved area, systemic toxicity. LRINEC score uses CRP, WCC, haemoglobin, sodium, creatinine and glucose; score 6 to 7 raises suspicion, 8 or above is high risk. Management: immediate surgical exploration and debridement, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics with clindamycin (toxin suppression) plus piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem and vancomycin for MRSA cover, aggressive resuscitation, ICU admission. Imaging should not delay surgery.
key_points: Pain out of proportion is the cardinal early sign
LRINEC score: 6-7 suspicion, 8+ high risk
Clindamycin for toxin suppression in addition to broad cover
Imaging must not delay surgical exploration
explanation.pearls: Type II necrotising fasciitis (group A Streptococcus) classically affects healthy patients after minor trauma; type I is polymicrobial in diabetes and surgical sites and includes Fournier gangrene.

subtopic_detail: Community-acquired pneumonia CURB-65 site of care
stem: A 72-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 3 days of productive cough, fevers, and dyspnoea. He has type 2 diabetes and hypertension. He lives alone and is independent at baseline. On examination he is alert with focal right basal crepitations, oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air, and a respiratory rate of 32. Chest x-ray confirms right lower lobe consolidation. He has not previously had pneumonia and has no known drug allergies.

data_table.Examination: Right basal crackles; no signs of consolidation outside; alert; mildly confused (AMTS 8/10)
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18.2 x10^9/L, CRP 162, urea 9.4 mmol/L, Cr 110 micromol/L, BSL 12.4 mmol/L; CXR: right lower lobe consolidation; lactate 1.8 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate site of care and empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Discharge with oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily for 5 days and general practitioner review in 48 hours
options.rationale: CURB-65 here is at least 4 (confusion, urea over 7, RR at least 30, BP under 90/60-borderline, age 65+), placing the patient at high risk and mandating inpatient management. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - CAP)

options.text: Admit to short-stay unit on oral amoxicillin-clavulanate with planned discharge within 24 hours of presentation
options.rationale: Short-stay with oral therapy is suited to low-to-moderate severity disease; this patient's vitals and biochemistry place him in moderate-to-severe CAP requiring intravenous therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - CAP)

options.text: Admit to general medical ward on intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g 6-hourly plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily
options.rationale: Moderate-severity CAP in an Australian inpatient is treated with IV benzylpenicillin plus an atypical-cover agent such as doxycycline; SMART-COP can refine ICU referral but ward admission is appropriate when oxygen and perfusion are correctable. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - CAP)

options.text: Admit to intensive care unit with intravenous meropenem and intravenous vancomycin to cover all resistant organisms
options.rationale: Empiric meropenem and vancomycin are reserved for severe CAP with risk factors for resistant pathogens or in immunocompromise; this presentation lacks those features. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - CAP)

options.text: Admit to general medical ward on intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily plus oral azithromycin 500 mg daily for 5 days
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone is reserved for moderate-severe CAP with intolerance or local resistance concerns; the Australian first-line in moderate disease is IV benzylpenicillin plus an oral atypical agent. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - CAP)

explanation.summary: Australian CAP management uses CURB-65 (or SMART-COP) to direct site of care. Score 0 to 1 typically outpatient with oral amoxicillin; 2 inpatient on oral or IV therapy; 3 or more inpatient with IV therapy and consider ICU. Moderate CAP empiric therapy is IV benzylpenicillin with an oral atypical agent (doxycycline preferred over macrolide in Australia for stewardship). Severe disease or septic shock prompts ceftriaxone plus azithromycin and ICU.
key_points: CURB-65 of 3 or more = inpatient IV therapy
AU first line moderate CAP: IV benzylpenicillin + doxycycline
SMART-COP refines ICU referral
Doxycycline preferred over azithromycin for atypical cover in AU
explanation.pearls: CURB-65 in this case: confusion + urea over 7 + RR over 30 + age 65+ = 4 - inpatient IV therapy mandated; AU first line is benzylpenicillin + doxycycline.

sources.label: TSANZ Position Statement: Community-acquired pneumonia in adults

subtopic_detail: Native valve infective endocarditis - empiric therapy
stem: A 58-year-old man with a history of degenerative aortic valve disease presents with 10 days of fevers, malaise, weight loss and a new exertional breathlessness. Examination reveals a soft pansystolic murmur not previously documented, splinter haemorrhages in two fingernails and microscopic haematuria on dipstick. Three sets of blood cultures are drawn from separate sites before any antibiotic is given. He has no penicillin allergy and is haemodynamically stable.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.4, HR 96, BP 118/64, RR 18, SpO2 96 percent room air
data_table.Examination: New apical pansystolic murmur, two splinter haemorrhages, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: WCC 14.2, CRP 142, creatinine 96, urinalysis 2+ blood 1+ protein, ECG sinus tachycardia, transthoracic echo pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empiric intravenous antibiotic regimen while cultures incubate?

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily as single-agent empiric therapy for community-acquired endocarditis
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone monotherapy does not cover staphylococci or enterococci adequately for native valve endocarditis empiric therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Endocarditis)

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.8 g every 4 hours plus flucloxacillin 2 g every 4 hours plus gentamicin 1 mg/kg every 8 hours
options.rationale: Triple therapy with benzylpenicillin, flucloxacillin and low-dose gentamicin gives appropriate coverage of streptococci, methicillin-susceptible staphylococci and enterococci pending culture and susceptibility results. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Endocarditis)

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading dose alone, withholding any beta-lactam until culture identification is available
options.rationale: Vancomycin monotherapy delays optimal beta-lactam therapy for susceptible organisms and is reserved for severe beta-lactam allergy or suspected methicillin-resistant infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Endocarditis)

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 1 g every 8 hours pending culture results given clinical stability and the prolonged subacute history
options.rationale: Endocarditis requires intravenous therapy regardless of clinical stability; oral therapy cannot achieve adequate bactericidal valve concentrations. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Endocarditis)

options.text: Intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 6 hours as broad spectrum gram-negative cover for the subacute fever syndrome
options.rationale: Piperacillin-tazobactam targets gram-negative and anaerobic pathogens that are not the primary cause of native valve endocarditis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Endocarditis)

explanation.summary: Empiric therapy for native valve endocarditis covers viridans streptococci, Staphylococcus aureus and enterococci because these account for the majority of cases. Combination therapy of benzylpenicillin plus flucloxacillin plus gentamicin is the Australian guideline regimen pending culture identification. Three separate sets of blood cultures from different venepuncture sites before antibiotics are essential to meet the Duke microbiological criterion. Modified Duke criteria combine clinical, microbiological and echocardiographic findings to support diagnosis. Streamlining of therapy occurs once organism and susceptibilities are known.
key_points: Three separate blood culture sets before antibiotics.
Cover staph, strep and enterococci empirically.
Benzylpenicillin plus flucloxacillin plus gentamicin in Australia.
Vancomycin replaces beta-lactams only for severe allergy or MRSA suspicion.
Streamline once organism and MIC are known.
explanation.pearls: Gentamicin 1 mg/kg every 8 hours uses the synergy dose, not the once-daily 5-7 mg/kg dose used for gram-negative sepsis; trough should be below 1 mg/L within 5 days of starting.

sources.label: ESC 2023 Guidelines for the management of endocarditis

subtopic_detail: Acute management of severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes
stem: You are the medical registrar called to the emergency department to assess a 68-year-old man with chronic kidney disease stage 3 on perindopril. Routine bloods done by the GP this morning returned a potassium of 6.7 mmol/L. An ECG taken on arrival shows peaked T waves throughout the precordial leads, reduced P wave amplitude and a QRS duration of 110 ms. He is alert and asymptomatic.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 152/86, HR 64 regular, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Alert and oriented; chest clear; no focal neurology; no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 6.7 mmol/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, urea 14 mmol/L, creatinine 220 micromol/L (baseline 150), bicarbonate 18 mmol/L; ECG: peaked T waves, low P, QRS 110 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Intravenous calcium gluconate 10 percent 10 mL over 2-5 minutes with continuous cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes (peaked T, P attenuation, QRS widening) requires immediate cardiac membrane stabilisation; calcium gluconate works in minutes and is the first step. (Source: KDIGO Acute Kidney Injury Guidelines)

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol 20 mg alone as the sole urgent intervention to lower potassium now
options.rationale: Salbutamol shifts potassium intracellularly but does not stabilise the myocardium; it follows calcium when ECG changes are present. (Source: KDIGO Acute Kidney Injury Guidelines)

options.text: Oral cation exchange resin alone with planned outpatient repeat in 24-48 hours' time
options.rationale: Cation exchange resins remove potassium slowly and are inadequate when ECG changes are present and the K is 6.7. (Source: KDIGO Acute Kidney Injury Guidelines)

options.text: Intravenous insulin and dextrose alone without prior calcium for myocardial stabilisation
options.rationale: Insulin and dextrose shift potassium effectively but do not stabilise the myocardium; calcium should precede them when ECG changes are evident. (Source: KDIGO Acute Kidney Injury Guidelines)

options.text: Cease perindopril alone with a planned repeat potassium check in 48 hours' time
options.rationale: Stopping the ACE inhibitor addresses the cause but does not treat the immediate cardiac risk from severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes. (Source: KDIGO Acute Kidney Injury Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes is a medical emergency. Management proceeds in three steps: stabilise the myocardium with intravenous calcium gluconate within minutes; shift potassium intracellularly using insulin with dextrose and nebulised salbutamol; and remove potassium from the body using diuresis, cation exchange resin or dialysis. Reversible causes including ACE inhibitor or potassium-sparing diuretic therapy should be addressed and follow-up potassium checks scheduled.
key_points: Calcium gluconate stabilises the myocardium within minutes.
Insulin-dextrose and salbutamol shift potassium intracellularly.
Resin or dialysis removes potassium from the body.
Cease ACE inhibitor and review longer-term causes.
explanation.pearls: Calcium gluconate has a shorter duration than the potassium shift you generate, so repeat ECGs after 30-60 minutes; an evolving QRS or sine wave despite shifts means it is time for dialysis, not another insulin bolus.

stem: A 58-year-old man presents for review 3 months after being diagnosed with an unprovoked left popliteal deep vein thrombosis. He was commenced on apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days followed by 5 mg twice daily. He has had no bleeding complications. His repeat ultrasound shows partial recanalisation of the thrombus. He has no personal or family history of VTE, no recent immobility, surgery, or malignancy. Age-appropriate cancer screening has been completed and is unremarkable.

data_table.Examination: Mild residual left calf swelling, no signs of post-thrombotic syndrome
data_table.Investigations: FBC normal, UEC normal, LFTs normal, age-appropriate cancer screening negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulation plan?

options.text: Continue apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily as extended secondary prevention
options.rationale: After completing initial anticoagulation for unprovoked VTE, extended anticoagulation is recommended if bleeding risk is acceptable. The AMPLIFY-EXT trial demonstrated that apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily provides effective secondary prevention with a bleeding rate comparable to placebo. In a patient with unprovoked DVT and no contraindications, extended therapy at the reduced prevention dose is the standard Australian approach. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology; AMPLIFY-EXT trial)

options.text: Cease anticoagulation after the completed 3-month course with surveillance
options.rationale: Unprovoked VTE carries a recurrence rate of approximately 10% at 1 year and 30% at 5 years after stopping anticoagulation. Current guidelines recommend extended anticoagulation for unprovoked events when bleeding risk is low, rather than stopping after 3 months. Stopping is appropriate for provoked VTE with a transient reversible risk factor. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology; BMJ Best Practice: VTE)

options.text: Switch to warfarin with a target INR of 2.0-3.0 for extended prophylaxis
options.rationale: Warfarin is effective for VTE prevention but is inferior to DOACs in convenience and safety for most patients. It requires regular INR monitoring, has numerous drug and food interactions, and the DOAC extended prevention trials showed better or equivalent efficacy with less bleeding. Switching a stable patient from apixaban to warfarin is not recommended. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology)

options.text: Reduce apixaban to 2.5 mg twice daily for 3 months then cease entirely
options.rationale: Reducing the dose for a fixed additional 3 months then stopping is not the recommended approach. The benefit of extended anticoagulation persists only while the patient remains on therapy. The risk of recurrence returns to baseline after cessation. Guidelines recommend ongoing extended therapy or indefinite treatment with annual reassessment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology; BMJ Best Practice: VTE)

options.text: Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily indefinitely at the treatment dose level
options.rationale: Continuing at the full treatment dose (5 mg twice daily) for extended prevention is not supported by evidence. The AMPLIFY-EXT trial showed the reduced dose of 2.5 mg twice daily was equally effective for recurrence prevention with significantly less bleeding than the full treatment dose. Dose reduction to 2.5 mg twice daily is the standard for extended therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology; BMJ Best Practice: VTE)

explanation.summary: Unprovoked VTE carries a high recurrence risk after anticoagulation cessation. Extended anticoagulation at a reduced DOAC dose is recommended when bleeding risk is acceptable. The decision to continue beyond the initial treatment period should be reassessed annually, balancing recurrence risk against bleeding risk. Age-appropriate cancer screening is recommended for unprovoked VTE to exclude occult malignancy.
key_points: Unprovoked VTE has approximately 10% annual recurrence after stopping anticoagulation
Apixaban 2.5 mg BD is the evidence-based extended prevention dose (AMPLIFY-EXT)
Extended therapy benefit persists only while on treatment
Annual reassessment of risk-benefit balance is recommended for ongoing therapy
explanation.pearls: The AMPLIFY-EXT trial showed apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily reduced VTE recurrence by 67% compared with placebo, with major bleeding rates indistinguishable from placebo at 0.2%, establishing the reduced dose as the standard for extended secondary prevention.
